title: End-stage COPD with cor pulmonale — sudden worsening, peripheral edema
scenario_text: Mrs. Saroja Devi, a 78-year-old woman from a small town in southern Karnataka, has end-stage GOLD IV COPD (15-year history; non-smoker; longstanding biomass smoke exposure from chulha cooking) complicated by cor pulmonale and chronic peripheral edema. She is on home O2 24h (2L/min), inhaled triple therapy, oral morphine SR 10mg BD for refractory dyspnea (well tolerated for 3 months), and furosemide 40mg OD + spironolactone 25mg OD for cor pulmonale. Baseline mMRC 4, ECOG 3. Over the past 24 hours she has had sudden worsening of dyspnea (mMRC now 5 — breathless even at complete rest, struggles to speak), pronounced increase in bilateral leg swelling, abdominal distension (mild ascites suspected), and decreased urine output. No fever, no purulent sputum, no productive cough beyond baseline. SpO2 on her usual O2 86% (baseline 90%), HR 110 irregular (suspected new AF), BP 95/60, RR 28, JVP elevated, bilateral basal crackles + wheeze. She was admitted to district hospital 4 weeks ago for similar but milder episode; preference clearly documented for home-based care, refuses ICU, accepts NIV at home if helpful. Daughter (lives next door) and daughter-in-law (lives with patient) are the caregivers. The visiting ASHA worker calls the helpline — patient is in distress, leg swelling is worse, what is happening, what to do at home?

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: End-stage GOLD IV COPD with cor pulmonale and chronic right heart failure (biomass smoke aetiology); chronic hypoxic respiratory failure
comorbidities: Cor pulmonale with chronic right heart failure

presenting_complaint: Acute-on-chronic dyspnea with worsening edema, mild ascites, hypotension, suspected new AF, and decreased urine output in end-stage COPD with cor pulmonale.
asker_query: Madam, aunty's breathing has become much worse since yesterday, legs are very swollen, stomach is also bigger, urine is less, heart is beating fast and irregular. Family does not want hospital. What is happening, what can we do at home, what medicines to adjust?
ideal_response_components: Frame the clinical picture — this is acute decompensation of cor pulmonale in end-stage COPD; the differential includes worsening right heart failure (most likely), new-onset atrial fibrillation contributing to decompensation, occult pulmonary embolism, silent infection (no fever does not exclude), pneumothorax (sudden onset), and disease progression to end of life. Given documented goals (no hospital, no ICU), the management must be a thoughtful home-based palliative approach with explicit decision points.

Symptom-priority management at home: (a) Optimise oxygen — increase to 3 L/min temporarily to target SpO2 88-92%, monitor for CO2 retention drowsiness (in cor pulmonale less restrictive than pure COPD); (b) Increase morphine for dyspnea — Morphine IR 2.5-5mg PO every 1-2h PRN for crisis dyspnea, plus increase SR background by 25% to 15mg BD; (c) Sit her upright; fan; reassurance.

Heart failure management: (a) Increase furosemide to 40mg PO BD or give furosemide 40mg SC stat (subcutaneous furosemide is feasible at home, effective for refractory edema in palliative cor pulmonale); (b) Continue spironolactone; (c) Restrict fluid intake to ~1 L/day; salt restriction.

Address the new irregular tachycardia: at the bedside, consider whether suspected AF needs rate control — gentle low-dose digoxin 62.5-125 mcg PO OD is a reasonable home-based choice (renally safer, also has positive effect in cor pulmonale); avoid beta-blockers in acute COPD decompensation; if rate ventricular rate is uncontrolled and contributing to distress, consult palliative team. Anticoagulation decision in palliative phase is shared with family — balance bleed risk vs stroke risk; in PPS 30% with limited life expectancy, often not initiated.

Address ascites/edema mechanically: gentle compression stockings if tolerated, elevate legs at rest, skin care (oedematous skin breaks down easily — emollients, no friction); if ascites is symptomatic and large, paracentesis at the 12-km palliative unit is an option.

Rule out reversible contributors that change management: (a) Send a CBC/CRP/UA from home or via local lab — silent infection (UTI or chest); empirical course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 625mg TDS x 5 days reasonable if clinical concern; (b) Consider whether new AF triggered by hypoxia improving with oxygen; (c) PE — unable to confirm at home, low D-dimer threshold for empirical LMWH only if life expectancy supports.

Anticipatory crisis kit at bedside: pre-emptive SC morphine 2.5mg PRN, SC midazolam 2.5mg PRN, SC glycopyrronium 0.2mg PRN for any terminal secretions, SC haloperidol 0.5mg PRN for delirium; written instructions to daughter on use.

Goals-of-care reaffirmation: this presentation may be terminal — discuss with family. She has preferred home; refuses ICU; the 24-72h trajectory may be improvement on optimised home regimen OR continued decline. Both pathways are honoured.

Practical family education: monitor SpO2, RR, urine output, swelling daily; recognise comfort vs distress; helpline 24/7 for any acute change; do NOT call ambulance for hospital transfer unless family changes mind.

Plan: home palliative team visit TODAY or tomorrow (12 km); bring SC kit, recheck on the diuretic and morphine titration, consider portable ECG and CXR for diagnostic confirmation if it changes management.

Acknowledge to daughter and daughter-in-law that this may be a dying episode — gentle preparation, presence, family rituals (Hindu/Karnataka — tulsi water, mantras, family gathering); ensure they know to call helpline and stay with her.
expected_guideline_citations: GOLD 2024 Report — Acute exacerbations and end-of-life care
ATS/ERS Statement on Optimum Symptom Treatment in Advanced COPD (2017)
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care (2nd ed.) — Cardiopulmonary failure at end of life
safety_traps: Pushing oxygen flow >4 L/min without monitoring CO2 retention symptoms (drowsiness, confusion) in COPD.
Adding beta-blocker for tachycardia in acute COPD decompensation (bronchospasm risk).
Aggressive IV diuresis without monitoring electrolytes / pre-renal AKI.
Sending the patient to hospital against documented goals — contrary to autonomy and her stated preference.
Reflexive anticoagulation for new AF in PPS 30% without balancing bleed risk and goals.
Missing the differential of PE or pneumothorax — keep these in mind but accept diagnostic limitations at home.
Failing to prepare the family for the possibility this is a terminal decompensation.
indian_context_notes: Biomass smoke COPD in women (cooking on chulha) is a major Indian phenomenon — under-diagnosed and frequently severe.
Subcutaneous furosemide for home palliation is increasingly used in Indian palliative units (Pallium India, KMC Manipal) — feasible and effective.
Digoxin remains widely used and affordable in India — NLEM available; rate-control role in palliative AF appropriate.
Kannada-Tamil bilingual region of southern Karnataka — ASHA should communicate clearly with family in their preferred language.
Refusal of hospital/ICU is increasingly common in informed Indian palliative patients — document with family witnesses.
12-km palliative unit (likely an IAPC-affiliated centre or major hospital with palliative service) is within range for home visit and crisis support.
